lines.text: Today you meet the dictionary, a way to store pairs of information, like names and numbers in a phone book.
A dictionary stores pairs, just like a phone book stores a name and a number.
The first part is the key and the second is the value. capitals = {"Kerala": "Thiruvananthapuram"} holds one pair.
capitals["Kerala"] gives the value stored for that key.
Keys must match exactly, so "kerala" with a small k is a different key.
Asking for a key that is not there gives a KeyError.
menu["idli"] = 30 adds a new pair if idli is not there yet.
If it is already there, the old value is replaced.
Use "idli" in menu to check before you look something up.
for item, price in menu.items(): visits every pair.
Each time round, item holds the key and price holds the value. len(menu) tells you how many pairs there are.
Curly brackets make a dictionary, and a colon joins each key to its value.
We look up Gujarat by its key, and Python finds the capital straight away.
Idli was not on the menu, so this line adds a brand new pair.
Chai was already there, so its price is replaced with twelve rupees.
The items method hands us one key and one value at a time.
This is how a canteen app could print its whole price list.
The class voted for its favourite fruit, and we start with an empty dictionary.
A new fruit gets a count of one, and a fruit we have seen before goes up by one.
Pizza is not a key in this dictionary, so Python stops with a KeyError.
Check first with if pizza in menu, or use the get method with a default value.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
